stories.title: Ahern questions logic over Commission's Drumcree decision
stories.summary: Former taoiseach Bertie Ahern has said that it was clear a month ago where the dispute over the Drumcree parade was going and the Parades Commission decision was made far too tight to the deadline for the march. "You would have to question the logic of that given the expected response from the Garvaghy Road residents. It was obvious ... the Garvaghy Road residents haven't changed their position." Mr Ahern said the effort should be to see if there is a resolution to the stand-off. He cautioned that if political parties in Northern Ireland think they will make some short-term gain out of winning a few votes based on reverting to the past, they will regret that. The Parades Commission, he said, was not the correct place for the Orange Order to bring a new proposal on the march. "What you needed was to try to see if there was a basis where you could have built up some confidence around seeing what the possibilities were between the residents and the Portadown Order.

stories.title: EU ministers to discuss energy-saving measures in Dublin
stories.summary: European energy ministers are to hold talks in Dublin tomorrow as the EU looks to cushion the impact of soaring energy prices ahead of a winter that promises to be difficult for consumers. Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen wrote to the 27 member states ahead of the meeting recommending measures to reduce demand for electricity and gas to help contain prices. "I invite you to consider taking or continuing to take measures that can... reduce gas and electricity demand for as long as necessary," he wrote in the letter, seen by AFP. The informal talks, which will be chaired by Minister for Climate, Energy, and the Environment Darragh O'Brien - under Ireland's Presidency of the EU - are not expected to result in major decisions, but will help coordinate action among the bloc's nations. European gas prices have more than doubled owing to the US-Iran war, just as Europe needs to replenish its reserves with winter beckoning. And Brussels wants to avoid countries rushing to fill up their reserves all together as families prepare to turn on their heaters - at the risk of driving prices up further.

stories.title: Australian firm to buy 35% in Daft and DoneDeal owner
stories.summary: An Australian digital advertising business specialising in property, REA Group is to pay €248 million on acquiring a 35% shareholding in Irish digital marketplace operator, Distilled that operates daft.ie and DoneDeal.ie. The proposed deal by the REA Group - which is the owner of Australia's realestate.com.au - and Distilled announced earlier this morning puts a value on the entire Distilled business of €708.57 million. The €708.57 million value on Distilled is an €84.57m increase on the €624m value placed on Distilled almost two years ago when Adevinta sold its 50pc stake in Distilled Ltd for €312m to Dublin based fund manager Blacksheep Fund Management in November 2024. However, since then, the leading multi-vertical digital marketplace operator, Distilled has expanded and has paid out €107.5m to purchase three businesses in Northern Ireland and the Republic over the last 14 months. As a result, since expanding beyond the Republic of Ireland, Daft.ie now accounts for under 30% of the Distilled business. In a statement today, the REA Group stated that "the proposed investment represents a strategically compelling transaction for REA and its shareholders with a disciplined entry into an attractive, high-growth market".

stories.title: Use of Russian assets should be 'kept on table' - McEntee
stories.summary: The Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee has said the issue of several hundred billion euro in frozen Russian assets should be "kept on the table" as the EU looks for ways to meet Ukraine's defence needs as winter approaches. Some €210bn in Russian central bank assets were immobilised just days after the invasion on Ukraine in February 2022, around €185bn of which remain held in a Belgian securities depository - Euroclear. Last December, EU leaders failed to convince Belgium to agree to allow the assets to be used to underwrite a long-term loan to meet Ukraine’s military and budget needs. Instead, the EU agreed the issuance of joint debt to the tune of €90bn for Ukraine over three years, using the enhanced cooperation mechanism to side-step objections by Hungary. However, given the intensity of Russia’s attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, and the prospect of a wholesale assault on the country’s energy infrastructure during the winter months, senior EU figures have suggested the frozen Russian assets should be revisited. Ukraine has signalled a shortfall of €27bn in its defence budget, as it struggles to meet a much more intensive aerial assault by Moscow using jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles.

stories.title: Ward's new assistant Sorensen named Villa interim boss
stories.summary: Carla Ward's new Republic of Ireland assistant coach Brian Sorensen has been named interim boss of WSL side Aston Villa following the sacking of Natalia Arroyo. Gary Cronin departed as Ward's backroom staff in August, leaving a vacancy that had to be filled with the Girls in Green heading towards a crucial World Cup play-off semi-final against Kazakhstan. Former Everton manager Sorensen - who is currently a technical advisor at Villa - got the nod. However events in Birmingham outfit today have increased his commitments at the club and raised questions about his availability for the upcoming Irish camp. Sorensen will be in the dugout for Wednesday's Subway Players Cup tie against Newcastle. Villa then have a league game against Crystal Palace on Sunday, the day before Ireland fly out to Astana for the first lef of the play-off. Ward managed Villa for three years, stepping away from the job in 2024. At her squad announcement press conference on Tuesday morning, she was effusive in her praise of the experienced Dane.

stories.summary: Leinster GAA will this week look to refine their proposal for a new senior inter-county hurling provincial championship of eight teams amid an extended structure. Former GAA president Nickey Brennan is chairing a special workgroup reviewing the structure of the Leinster Senior Hurling Championship to help developing counties achieve more meaningful access to elite competition The aim is to make the Leinster series as competitive as possible and lift developing teams who face steep challenges bridging the gap to higher terrain. From an early stage the plan was always set to consider expanding the current six-team round-robin format into an eight-team competition divided into groups. Factoring in the progress made by 2025 Joe McDonagh Cup champions Kildare – even though they experienced immediate relegation this season – was also a priority for the committee.

stories.title: City CEO issues defiant message to European club bosses
stories.summary: Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano has told his fellow European club bosses the already lengthy legal battle with the Premier League will take "a lot more time" to conclude. News broke on Friday that City had been found guilty of all but one of 115 charges they faced of breaching the league's financial rules, immediately sparking speculation they could face unprecedented sanctions. City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak told supporters in an open letter published on Saturday that the club were "confident" of proving their innocence, and chief executive Soriano addressed the elephant in the room when he met fellow members of the European Football Clubs board in Copenhagen on Monday. The Press Association understands Soriano said at the end of the EFC board meeting that he felt he had to say something given Friday’s news, that City disagreed with the ruling but remained confident of winning and that the club were still fighting. Sources in the meeting said Soriano then remarked: "It’s taken eight years to get here, and it’s going to take a lot more time." The "eight years" Soriano referred to was the opening of the league’s investigation into City in 2018.

stories.title: McMillan: Work needed to get Munster fans back on side
stories.summary: Munster head coach Clayton McMillan says he and his players have to "work" to get some supporters back on board, but the New Zealander is confident with their direction of travel, despite Saturday's 26-20 defeat to Glasgow Warriors. The province let a 20-14 lead slip in the final quarter at Thomond Park, as they lost what McMillan described as an "arm-wrestle" against a powerful Scottish side. Despite the defeat, there were clear positives in the performance, notably through 21-year-old scrum-half Ben O'Donovan, and new signing Kieran Brookes. A modest crowd of just over 11,000 turned up at Thomond Park for what should have been an attractive fixture, with a 5.30pm kick-off against one of the league's best sides. And the Munster coach acknowledged they are in the process of repairing the relationship with some fans after a chaotic season last year. "I think for the people that were here, I hope that they saw something in the team to be optimistic about," McMillan (below) said on Saturday night.

stories.title: My TV and me - why I just can't let go of my old telly
stories.summary: Sixteen years, four house moves and one brief separation: that's how long my so-called dumb TV and I have been together. At this point it would be hard to imagine life without my Panasonic TX-P42S20L. But I know the day will come when I can't switch it on anymore. Okay, Plasma televisions use a lot of power (275W) compared to your modern day so-called Smart TVs (60W). But what do you buy a TV for? Yes, the picture. Much of my viewing is either SD or HD, skewing towards classic and black & white cinema. The blacks on a plasma TV are top notch. Though the likes of OLED (organic light-emitting diode) blacks can be technically lovely, at least on high end models, I still find myself often struggling with a twentieth century cinema through twenty first century technology. One day, I swapped out the plasma for the 'Smart' 4K LED television in my office. After a few movie viewings on the satellite channel Talking Pictures – the go to place these days for forgotten '60s and '70s films and shows - this experiment ended up being a one-night stand. Even with all the bells and whistle settings turned off it just looked…off. I retuned the LED to the office and put my ‘dumb’ Plasma back on the pedestal in the living room where it deserved to be. CRT and Plasma televisions are officially extinct. It you have a working model, treat it with care, because one day, no matter how hard you press the button, it will all be over. As much as we’re now a confirmed couple for life, I confess I do have a side thing going. My CRT (Cathode ray tube) television gets rolled out on special occasions. Mostly to watch old video tapes. Indeed, CRT and VHS tend to come as a couple, especially for old episodes of Doctor Who. Have you ever tried playing back a VHS tape on a high-definition television? The results are, well, passable. It kind of looks like the TV is insulted that you’re trying to push something into a slot which wasn’t really designed for that, and does the bare minimum so you won’t try it again.

stories.title: Saved by the Bell star Dennis Haskins dies aged 75
stories.summary: Saved By The Bell actor Dennis Haskins, who played school principal Richard Belding in the hit US sitcom, has died aged 75. His co-star Lark Voorhies remembered him as "a loyal friend" and said knowing him for almost 40 years had been "one of the truest blessings" of her life. Haskins' agent Jay Schachter confirmed his death in a statement to US media. A cause of death was not given. Voorhies, who played Lisa Turtle in Saved By The Bell, paid tribute to the actor on Instagram. "We shared so much history together from our earliest days, and through it all, he remained a fabulous person, a loyal friend, and someone with such a kind, gentle heart," she wrote. "I am truly heartbroken by his passing and will miss his warmth and laughter more than words can say.

stories.title: Harrisson Gardner on how to prepare your home for emergencies
stories.summary: From storms and flooding to power outrages and managing extreme temperatures, Irish households have has more challenges to contend with in recent years. Two years after the record-breaking Storm Éowyn, which left a trail of devastation and some Irish homes without power for three weeks, many of us will be thinking more about how to plan for a future of similar events. Harrisson Gardner has put his 15 years of experience building off grid homes and teaching building skills into his new book, Heat, Shelter, Water, Food: How to be Ready for the Unexpected. He told McCullagh that the storm is what inspired him to start writing this book, as he knew he had these skills but felt he had gotten "complacent" about passing them on. He calls how "messy" things got in his home during the storm, as they lost power and water and also battled a vomiting bug. "It's not meant to foster fear", he says of his book, "it's meant to respond to a bit of the anxiety that people might already be feeling." There are some challenges that we can't control, like rising temperatures during summer months, increasing fuel prices and hosepipe bans that limit how we can use water, he adds. "I think that in general people are realising that we're a lot more reliant than we realise for things that are actually our basic human needs. These are the things that we need to survive."

stories.title: Man, woman charged with perjury over McGregor appeal
stories.summary: A man and a woman have been charged with perjury following an investigation by gardaí into evidence filed in Conor McGregor's failed appeal against a civil court jury’s finding that he raped Nikita Hand. Samantha O’Reilly and Steven Cummins were brought before Dublin District Court this morning. They have been charged with giving statements in a judicial proceeding which were false and which they knew to be false. Detective Sergeant Maria Cassells told the court Ms O’Reilly, who is 38, was arrested at the couple’s home in Cherry Orchard Green in Dublin this morning. She has been charged with two counts of giving false statements in January and May last year. Detective Garda Padraic Hanley told the court Mr Cummins, who is 39, was also arrested at home this morning. He has been charged with one count of giving a false statement in January 2025. Judge Michele Finan was told the DPP has directed that they both be tried before a jury in the Circuit Criminal Court.

stories.title: Rise in prescription opioid use under public drug scheme
stories.summary: Approximately 1.5 million people, or around 30% of the population, are eligible for the General Medical Services (GMS) scheme, the country's main community drug scheme. Between 2018 and 2025, the State spent €316m on opioid prescriptions across the GMS and two other community drug schemes: the Long Term Illness (LTI) scheme and the Drugs Payment Scheme (DPS). Most of this expenditure, €271m, was through the GMS. The annual number of opioid prescriptions across the three schemes increased by 18% between 2018 and 2025. On average, more than two million prescriptions were recorded each year. Prescription opioid use has come into sharp focus in recent decades because of the US opioid epidemic, which has been the subject of several high-profile television series, books and podcasts. While Ireland has not experienced problems on the same scale, the use of prescription opioids under the main community drug scheme has increased in recent years. The aggregated data covers prescription opioids including oxycodone, codeine, fentanyl, morphine and tramadol. It includes information on costs, patient numbers and prescribing across the HSE’s 32 former Local Health Office areas (LHOs).

stories.title: Budget 2027: A political battle to frame what comes next
stories.summary: Budgets might be all about the numbers, but how they add up for the public always comes down to framing. stories.title: Airlines can't keep fares low due to oil prices - O'Leary
stories.summary: Ryanair's O'Leary says airlines cannot keep fares low with current oil prices. Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary said today that demand for air travel remained very strong because airlines had kept fares low, but warned that this could not continue with oil prices at current levels. O'Leary said that jet fuel costs would push summer 2027 fares up by 15% to 20%. "We're optimistic for the future, but there's lots of short-term challenges, most notably what will happen with Trump and the Republicans in the midterm elections in November," he told Reuters in an interview. "We want to see a resolution of the war in Ukraine. We want to see a resolution of the war in the Middle East. We'd like everybody to get back to peace, love and air travel." Speaking at a press conference in Warsaw O’Leary also addresses possible delays in certification of Boeing Max planes.

stories.summary: Russian drones struck Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences in the historic heart of Kyiv today, in the latest deadly daytime attack on the Ukrainian capital. One person was killed and four others in attacks on Dnipro, in the south east. Kyiv has increasingly faced Russian drone and missile attacks as Europe's worst conflict since World War II grinds through its fifth year. Video footage shared online appeared to show a high-speed drone smashing into the National Academy of Sciences at a sharp angle, exploding and sending acrid smoke into the blue sky above. People were seen leaning out of windows as bright orange flames engulfed part of the building. Ukraine's former national security and defence council secretary Volodymyr Gorbulin told state broadcaster Suspilne that he was at work at the academy at the time and was slightly wounded.

stories.title: Retiring Grugan happy to complete Armagh circle
stories.summary: Rory Grugan's Armagh career started 15 years ago with 70 minutes of McKenna Cup action and his manager Paddy O'Rourke using his post-match media scrum to compare him to Marty Clarke. The Down leftie was one of the hottest names in football at the time, having come so close to dragging the Mourne County to a shock All-Ireland a few months previously. As far as potential player correlations go, it seemed a heavy burden to place on the Ballymacnab youngster. Now as the All-Ireland winner tries to adapt to life without county football - something that's been present in nearly half of his 35 years on this earth - O'Rourke can take solace from being right. Grugan was a linchpin of Armagh's acceleration under Kieran McGeeney, moving from a side that yo-yoed between Division 2 and 3 to being deemed one of the best in the country over the last five years, with Celtic Cross and Ulster medals to show for it. All things come to an end though and with Grugan and fellow 2009 All-Ireland Minor winner James Morgan departing, and more to come in the coming weeks, that 2024 team has lost a lot of names, albeit the Crossmaglen defender left the squad mid-season in '24 before returning last year. After the 2025 campaign, Stefan Campbell, Jemar Hall, Ciaron O'Hanlon (now coached by Clarke at Killeavy), Niall Rowland, Ciaran Higgins and Shane McPartlan all stepped away too.
stories.rssSummary: Rory Grugan's 15 years in orange brought with it many dark days, but when all was said and done, the Ballymacnab man had helped the Orchard County to ascend to the top of the game.

stories.title: Club wrap: Éire Óg dethroned; Moran to rescue in Mayo
stories.summary: Éire Og have been dethroned in Clare following a heavy 1-24 to 2-14 loss to Inagh-Kilnamona in Sunday's hurling semi-final. Inagh-Kilnamona led 0-14 to 0-07 at the break, but having had the aid of the breeze, it remained to be seen if it was enough of a cushion. In the end, it proved more than enough and after Marco Cleary had goaled midway through the second half to bring the Ennis side back to within six, Fred Hegarty struck back at the other end to ease them clear again. David Reidy did score a late goal for the holders, but they were second best on the day. Kilmaley await in the final after Saturday's win 0-25 to 1-11 against Scariff, a result that secured a first final spot for the club in 22 years. For only the second time since 2012, Kilcoo have lost a knock-out match in the Down SFC after a thrilling 4-16 to 1-20 defeat to perennial rivals Burren. The St Mary's side, who inflicted that other defeat in the 2012 decider, got off to a dream start with Ódhran Murdock converting two penalties in the opening quarter.

stories.title: Gakpo ankle injury adds to Liverpool injury concerns
stories.summary: Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo has withdrawn from international duty with the Netherlands after he sustained an ankle injury. The 27-year-old was forced off in the first half of their 2-1 Nations League victory over Serbia on Sunday evening following a challenge from Ipswich midfielder Sasa Lukic. Liverpool confirmed on Monday that Gakpo will now return to undergo further assessment from the club's medical staff. Gakpo, who has made a strong start to the season for the Reds with two goals and four assists, will now miss Nations League games against Greece and the return fixture with Serbia. The extent of Gakpo's injury is not yet known and it remains to be seen whether he will be in line to return for Liverpool's first game following the international break against Manchester City. The news serves as another blow for Andoni Iraola during the international break after striker Alexander Isak also returned to the club after he picked up a minor injury while playing for Sweden.

stories.title: Parsons breaks record as Ireland hold off Japan in Galway
stories.summary: Beibhinn Parsons became Ireland's record tryscorer, as Scott Bemand's side returned to winning ways in the WXV Global Series. The Galway native scored two tries on home soil at Dexcom Stadium to bring her Test tally to 24 for Ireland, on a day where Ireland just about had enough to edge a 31-24 win against a plucky Japan side. Bemand's side scored five tries in total, with Brittany Hogan also crossing twice, with one for Aoife Dalton, but several of the issues from last week's defeat to USA were again on display. Ireland were 19-0 in front approaching half time before their indiscipline allowed the opposition back into the game; Erin King picking up a yellow card and Japan scored two tries during that period, while they gave away a total of 16 penalties across the 80 minutes. Maul defence will also be a concern ahead of next week's rematch with Japan in Cork, as the Sakura XV used that avenue to score three of their four tries. While those issues will be a concern, Ireland's ability to grind through the second half will be a big positive, particularly into such a strong wind, while their scrum was largely dominant as they used Eilís Cahill and Linda Djougang to real effect, with Anna McGann exceptional in the centre.

stories.title: Ireland: Why it matters to be an island - the new book extracted
stories.summary: We present an extract from Ireland: Why it matters to be an island, the new book by Professor Michael Cronin. It is a simple fact that Ireland is an island nation. But how often do we consider what it means to be an islander? In his new book, Michael Cronin argues that we tend to ignore the fundamental fact of our island existence. For centuries, the question of this island's independence has centred on the politics of the place and an ability to own the land we stand on. But now, as the climate emergency threatens our shared island home, we need to urgently rethink how to protect and promote our island existence, on both land and at sea. Understanding islands differently entails asserting a sense of purpose and place in the world, retrieving a sense of solidarity across the globe with other islanders and a productive reckoning with our island status as an ocean people. No (hu)man is an island but every (hu)man on the island of Ireland is an islander. This simple fact is widely ignored in Irish life. If islandness or islands are ever discussed, it is always with reference to Ireland's offshore islands. The island itself becomes an imaginary mainland extending in all directions, obliterating the seas and ocean that encircle it on every side. The massive shift from sea to air travel in late-twentieth-century Ireland has made islandness feel increasingly abstract, a momentary glimpse of the sea by the air traveller before they disappear into cloudy oblivion. Using the term 'island’ in reference to ‘Ireland’ can feel loaded, as if any mention of the ‘island of Ireland’ were a declaration of republican manifest destiny, a surreptitious fusion of physical space with political sovereignty. The roots of this diminished sense of a sea-bound, island being are to be found in Irish history. The immiseration of the majority population, culminating in the Great Famine in the mid-nineteenth century, meant that the question of the land and of land ownership became paramount in modern Irish politics. Land, as a site of a historical dispossession and economic marginalisation, becomes sacred. There are Land Wars nineteenth-century Ireland but no Sea Wars. The colonial dispensation meant that, on the one hand, access to rivers and coastal waters became subject to a new regime of imperial surveillance and, on the other hand, coerced land transfers led to the rise of a nationalism that was ‘racy of the soil’ at the expense of all else. In other words, many inhabitants of the island were confronted with a dual schism: they were alienated from the possibilities of the sea and simultaneously distanced from possession of the land. The consequence was a project of national emancipation, primarily focused on the land, but on land that was disconnected from the sea. The terrestrial hold on the national imaginary meant that no integrated sense of island identity, where land and sea would figure equally, was possible. The dual fracture of the colonial period – loss of land, loss of sea – meant that the two primary functions of the sea were as a route out of the country in the form of migration and as a channel of trade for the agricultural produce of alienated labour that both financed and fed empire. The carefully programmed elision of the sea was not specific to the English. William Atkins, writing on the French colonisation of New Caledonia, refers to the sea as the highway for indigenous (Kanak) contact with the Polynesian world: ‘One effect of colonisation was to cut off this highway, quite literally to insulate Kanak society from the wider community of Oceania.’ Political subjugation, in the Irish case, did not, of course, mean the end of contact with the maritime world. Quite the contrary, as borne out by the experiences of mass emigration and by the rise of imperial trade. Yet the nature of the contact for the majority population would largely be on the coloniser’s terms rather than those of the colonised. Nel Pearson claims, for example, that, for all of the integration of Irish merchants and workforce and shipbuilding capacity into the nineteenth century, British maritime-world Irish sea history remained largely synonymous with dislocation, subordination and loss: The hunger for connection became apparent in Ireland's rapid integration into the global digital order in the closing decades of the twentieth century. This includes not only mass emigration before and after the Famine of the 1840s, but also legacies of artistic expropriation, disproportionate distribution of seaborne capital among Catholics and Protestants, English control of Irish ports from 1800 to 1938, and severe trade imbalances. Both Ian Friel, in his Maritime History of Britain and Ireland, and Christopher Harvie, in A Floating Commonwealth, point to Ireland's lack of its own merchant marine and England’s political subjugation of Ireland’s maritime industry and trade as key factors differentiating Irish modernisation from that of Scotland, Wales and England.

stories.title: First look at Andrew Scott is Oscar-tipped Elsinore
stories.summary: The first trailer for Andrew Scott's Oscar-tipped new film Elsinore has been released, offering an extended look at the Dublin actor’s acclaimed performance as Scottish stage star Ian Charleson. The biographical drama follows Charleson in the final months of his life as he prepares to play Hamlet at London’s National Theatre while seriously ill with Aids. Directed by Simon Stone and written by Pride screenwriter Stephen Beresford, Elsinore has already won the International People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival. Scott’s performance has also drawn strong reviews and generated awards-season buzz ahead of the film’s release. The trailer opens with Charleson frustrated by the direction of his career following his success as Olympic athlete and missionary Eric Liddell in the Oscar-winning 1981 film Chariots of Fire. Discussing his ambition to one day play Hamlet, he says: "It’s the greatest part you can play. In the greatest theatre."

stories.title: Is Honda's new hybrid sports coupe worth buying?
stories.summary: The return of the Honda Prelude revives a nameplate that enthusiasts have missed for decades. It has coupe styling, hybrid efficiency and everyday usability in a sleek two-door GT package. It's for buyers looking for a practical, fuel-efficient coupe to use as a daily driver. The latest Prelude may not be the traditional performance-focused rival it used to be, but is however a more hybrid-focused grand tourer. At a time when affordable two-door cars are rare, the Prelude fills a gap for drivers looking for a little performance, great looking aesthetics with comfort and efficiency at the pumps. Although with a 35 litre tank, we'd make sure to plan ahead when making longer trips.

stories.title: Minister to seek approval for boiler scrappage scheme
stories.summary: Minister for the Environment Darragh O'Brien is to seek Cabinet approval for a new boiler scrappage scheme. Grants of €2,000 are to be made available to scrap oil and kerosene boilers being replaced by heat pumps. This is in addition to the existing grant of up to €12,500 available for heat pumps, thereby bringing potential savings of up to €14,500 for households. Mr O'Brien is to tell his Cabinet colleagues of a new set of enhanced grants to help households and businesses reduce energy costs and move away from fossil fuels, with a €600 battery grant also to be made available. Mr O'Brien will argue how the new grants will help strengthen Ireland's energy security. Ministers will also discuss enhanced supports for households at risk of energy poverty. The new supports, developed through the work of the National Energy Affordability Taskforce (NEAT), include a range of improvements to the schemes administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) that will make it easier and more affordable for households and businesses to improve energy efficiency, install renewable energy technologies and switch to cleaner heating systems.

stories.title: Commission of investigation recommended into spinal care
stories.summary: A Government backed scoping report into the treatment of children with scoliosis and spina bifida at Children's Health Ireland (CHI) has recommended a commission of investigation rather than a public tribunal. The report recommends that the commission examine four areas including waiting lists, spinal surgery, hip dysplasia and a group of children who were not transferred from Our Lady’s Hospital Crumlin to Temple Street after 2008. It says a commission would primarily carry out its work in private, which it says would be more appropriate given that the issues concerning the medical treatment of children. It also says this approach may encourage broader participation from families and children who may otherwise be reluctant to take part in the process if it was conducted in public. The report says a commission would provide a more flexible and less adversarial framework and would be more efficient in terms of time and resources. However, the Spina Bifida and Hydrocephalus Paediatric Advocacy Group says that families of these children are no longer willing to allow the treatment of their children to be dealt with behind closed doors.

stories.title: Productivity 8 times lower in domestic vs foreign sector
stories.summary: Labour productivity stood at €125.3 per in Ireland in 2025, according to the latest figures from the Central Statistics Office. Labour productivity is defined as the output per hour worked and is a key indicator of economic efficiency and competitiveness. There was a significant difference in labour productivity in the domestic economy and in sectors dominated by foreign-owned companies: €65.8 per hour vs €507.3 per hour. Labour productivity across the economy increased by 6.1% last year, driven by the foreign-dominated sector, which saw labour productivity rise by 14.2%. Growth in gross value added (7.8%) outpaced growth in hours worked (1.6%). Remarkably, in the domestic sector labour productivity decreased by 0.8% last year, as hours worked grew faster than gross value added.

stories.title: Pope ends French trip with call for Europe to combat lies
stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV wrapped up a historic four-day visit to France today after warning that relations between nations were becoming increasingly uncivilised and urging Europe to help break the spiral of "lies and deceit". Speaking in the eastern city of Metz near the border with Germany, the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics did not mention any world leaders by name. The Pope sees Europe as a counterweight to major powers and has in the past called on the European Union to overcome tensions and rediscover unity in pursuit of peace in Ukraine and beyond. Leo, the first US pontiff, has clashed with President Donald Trump in recent months over the harsh crackdown on immigration in the United States and the war on Iran. "Relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilised. The value of keeping one's word is dismissed. Instead, people boast of lies and deceit," Leo said in French, alongside President Emmanuel Macron and a handful of other leaders. "Europe can help to break this cycle through the respect for others that it has learned to cultivate and preserve," Pope Leo said, on the first official papal visit to France in nearly two decades.

stories.title: Leinster need to bounce back after opening day defeat
stories.summary: It was a disappointing opening weekend of the United Rugby Championship for the Irish provinces. It is the first time in 17 years that all four teams have lost on the opening day of the season. Munster and Connacht were ahead for large periods of their respective games before frustratingly allowing those leads to slip away. Both struggled to hold on in the final quarter, highlighting some of the concerns around quality and squad depth in Irish rugby at present. Ulster, meanwhile, gave Edinburgh too much of a head start before launching their own fightback and coming within a score in a tight finish. The contrast between their start and finish will frustrate head coach Richie Murphy, but the fact that they finished the game playing their best rugby should provide some encouragement ahead of their second-round clash with Glasgow Warriors. Despite losing their opening fixture, Leinster will probably be the happiest of the four provinces after fighting to secure two points away to the Lions. Losing on the opening weekend immediately puts pressure on a team, and it will not get any easier for Leinster when they face the Sharks in the second round. However, there is plenty for Leo Cullen and his coaching staff to be pleased about. They have got the South African trip out of the way early in the season, and in many ways, this could be the perfect time to take an extended squad away for two fixtures.
